Who a caller **arrives as**, and who they **become** before the Data boundary.

`db/access.snapshot.md` is the other half and it commits the predicate —
`workspaceId != auth().workspaceId`. This commits the predicate's **input**.
A resolver that emits the wrong tenant changes no line of that file, so
without this one the whole API half of tenancy has no diffable face.

No values anywhere below. A claim's NAME is a fact about the application; a
claim's VALUE is a caller.

## Tenancy

**No `tenancy { }` block.** Nothing here is scoped to a tenant by declaration;
an app doing it in service where-clauses instead has no rule this file can read.

## Resolvers — `createApp({ principal })`

`standing` — a hand-written resolver, which describes nothing about
itself. The name is the whole of what is committed, so a change to which model
proves membership is invisible in this diff. Give it a `describe()` returning
`{ kind, model, subject, tenant, standing, claims, include }` — or a LIST of them,
one per source it composes (`FJS-D694`) — and the rows below fill in.

## Claims

What the resolvers may merge onto the principal, by name.

None described.
`userId` and `id` are refused by name: a claim says what a caller HOLDS for this
request, never who they are. Identity is `IAuth`'s and nothing else's.

## Standing

The resolver emits no standing, so every caller is graded by the session alone —
`getLevel` over what `IAuth` issued.

## What the tenant rules reach

| | Count | Models |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scoped by column | 0 | — |
| Scoped by delegation | 0 | — |
| Exempt — `@@tenant(none)` | 0 | — |

An exemption is a decision, so it is listed by name rather than counted. A model
moving into this row is a model every tenant can now read.

Whether these rules HOLD is a separate question with an executed answer —
litestone's `verifyTenantIsolation()`, which seeds a row for one tenant and has
another try to reach it.

## Refusals

Three ways a caller ends up with no tenant claim, and they are three different
sentences. `tenantClaimGuard` tells them apart by whether a resolver ran at all.

| Situation | Status | Whose problem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nothing in this app emits the claim | 403 | the developer's — no resolver is configured |
| The request named no tenant | 403 | the caller's — the request is incomplete |
| The request named one they do not belong to | 403 | the caller's — refused |

**403 in every branch, and 401 in none.** 401 means *you have not proved who you
are*, and the caller has — every client treats it as a dead token, so a member of
A following a link into B was not refused, they were signed out of A (`FJS-383`).

## Per-tenant configuration

The allow-list of configuration keys a tenant may override.

**None. This app installs no `createApp({ tenantConfig })`**, so everything it is
configured with resolves once at boot and is the same for every tenant: the mail
transport and its from-address, a bucket, a timezone, a locale, a branding value,
a rate limit.

That is a legitimate app. What it cannot do is be one deployment that several
customers each experience as theirs, where the customer-facing half of *theirs* is
mostly not rows.
